did_you_know.text: Did you know? Ezekiel’s prophecy concerning Egypt was delivered in the tenth year, in the tenth month, on the twelfth day of the month.
Did you know? Pharaoh is portrayed in the prophecy as a great dragon lying in the midst of the Nile and boasting, “My Nile is my own; I made it for myself.”
Did you know? The Lord describes capturing Pharaoh and the fish of his Nile with hooks and bringing them up from the Nile together.
Did you know? Egypt is compared to a staff made of reeds for the house of Israel—a support that appears helpful but breaks and injures the one who leans on it.
Did you know? The punishment of Egypt includes bringing a sword against it and eliminating both people and animals from the land.
Did you know? The land is described as desolate for forty years, so that neither human foot nor animal hoof will pass through it.
Did you know? After forty years, the Lord says that he will gather the Egyptians from the nations to which its people had been scattered.
Did you know? Even after Egypt is restored to Pathros, it will remain a “lowly kingdom” and will no longer exalt itself above the nations.
Did you know? In the later prophecy, Nebuchadnezzar’s army is described as having worked hard during the siege of Tyre, yet receiving no wages from it.
Did you know? At the end of the chapter, the Lord promises to make a horn sprout for the house of Israel and to give Ezekiel “an open mouth” among them, so that they may know that he is the Lord.
